newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO try to blunt bomb impact on talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO try to blunt bomb impact on talks.

text.p: Israel and the PLO sought on Friday to blunt the impact on faltering Middle East peace talks of two bombs that wounded 13 people in Tel Aviv.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to respond with "extreme severity" if the nail-packed bombs were proved to have been planted by Arabs from areas under the control of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
But Netanyahu immediately resumed talks, interrupted by the Thursday blasts, with U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross.
Arafat's aides also vowed to pursue negotiations, saying such violence was not in the interest of the self-rule Palestinian Authority.
Israeli police said they did not know who dropped the bombs in garbage cans near Tel Aviv's central bus station.
Netanyahu blamed "terrorists". Police said on Friday forensic evidence pointed to a terrorist act but they could not rule out a criminal gangland attack.
Netanyahu discussed the bombs at Friday's weekly cabinet meeting.
Israel's Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said on Friday he expected full security cooperation with Arafat "because we are all in favour of the peace process".

He told Israel radio that he did not believe the bombings were directly linked to the deadlock over an Israeli troop redeployment from Hebron and dates for further pullbacks in the occupied West Bank.
"I don't believe anyone is trying to speed up or thwart the signing by these attacks," Kahalani said. He said the bombs were of the kind used in Palestinian attacks in the 1970s and 1980s.

This has led some Israeli and Palestinian officials to speculate that small, secular Palestinian factions opposed to the Israel-PLO peace accords were behind the attacks rather than the larger Hamas or Islamic Jihad fundamentalist groups that have used suicide bombers over the past three years.

"I don't think Palestinians were behind these explosions because such attacks serve only Netanayhu," Palestinian Justice Minister Freih Abu Meddein told Reuters. Arafat fears that Netanyahu will cite violence as a reason for delaying the transfer of more of the West Bank to Palestinian rule.
Palestinian Authority member Sufyan Abu Zayda said Israel should not use the bombs as a pretext to clamp curfews and closures on Palestinian areas.
"The only way...is not severe restrictions but to make peace and sign an agreement," he said.
A deal on Israeli redeployment, agreed by the Labour government Netanyahu ousted last May, seems as elusive as ever.
But U.S. officials said Ross would continue his diplomatic shuttle and stay in the region for a meeting with Arafat on Saturday. Arafat left for Paris on Friday.

Palestinians have turned down a U.S. compromise date for West Bank troop withdrawals, insisting Washington make Israel respect the original timetable under which the three pullbacks should be completed by September.
